los.text: Identify, describe and label the three layers of meninges: the dura mater, the arachnoid mater, and the pia mater and the important structures relating to them.
los.html:
LayerStructureSpaces and features
Dura materTough outer layer; two layers in the skull, one in the spineExtradural space (potential in the skull, real in the spine with fat and veins); dural venous sinuses between its layers
Arachnoid materThin, avascular, lies against the duraSubdural space (potential; bridging veins cross it); arachnoid granulations project into the sinuses (CSF absorption)
Pia materDelicate, follows every sulcus; carries vesselsSubarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia: CSF, cerebral arteries; cisterns where it widens
  • Spinal cord: pia forms denticulate ligaments (anchor the cord laterally) and the filum terminale
    • cord ends at L1/2, dural sac at S2.
BleedSpaceVessel
ExtraduralBetween skull and duraMiddle meningeal artery (pterion)
SubduralBetween dura and arachnoidBridging veins
SubarachnoidUnder the arachnoidBerry aneurysm (circle of Willis), trauma
  • Meningitis inflames the arachnoid and pia (leptomeninges) and the CSF in between.

los.text: Describe the endosteal and meningeal layers of the dura mater, the four septa created by it dividing up the cranial cavity, and the relationship with the major venous sinuses (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, diaphragma sellae).
los.html:
• Cranial dura: endosteal layer (the periosteum of the skull, continuous with pericranium through foramina) and meningeal layer (continuous with the spinal dura).
    • They are fused except where they separate to enclose the dural venous sinuses, and where the meningeal layer folds inwards as septa.
SeptumPositionSinuses in its edges
Falx cerebriSickle between the cerebral hemispheres, attached to crista galli in frontSuperior sagittal (attached edge), inferior sagittal (free edge), straight sinus (where it meets the tentorium)
Tentorium cerebelliTent over the cerebellum, under the occipital lobes; free edge forms the tentorial notch around the midbrainTransverse sinuses (attached edge), superior petrosal sinuses, straight sinus
Falx cerebelliSmall midline fold between the cerebellar hemispheresOccipital sinus
Diaphragma sellaeRoof over the pituitary fossa, pierced by the stalkIntercavernous sinuses
HerniationUncus through the tentorial notch (compresses III → dilated pupil); cingulate gyrus under the falx; tonsils through the foramen magnum.
Nerve supplyDura is pain-sensitive (V above the tentorium, C1–3 and X below): headache.

los.text: Describe the anatomical structures encountered during the following procedures: lumbar puncture, spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthetic block, epidural (peridural) anaesthetic block. Explain the indications and risks associated with these techniques.
los.html:
ProcedureLevelLayers passedNeedle end point
Lumbar punctureL3/4 or L4/5 (Tuffier's line at L4)Skin, fat, supraspinous, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoidSubarachnoid space (CSF drips back)
Spinal (subarachnoid) blockSame, below L1/2SameSubarachnoid space: small dose of anaesthetic mixes with CSF
Epidural blockAny level (lumbar for labour)Up to ligamentum flavum, then loss of resistanceEpidural space (outside the dura); catheter left in
Lumbar punctureSpinal blockEpidural
UsesDiagnose meningitis, SAH (xanthochromia), measure pressure, give drugsCaesarean section, lower limb and lower abdominal surgeryLabour analgesia, post-operative pain relief, surgery
Onset / dosen/aFast, dense, small doseSlower, larger volume, can be topped up
RisksPost-dural puncture headache, infection, bleeding, coning if raised ICP with a mass (CT first)Hypotension (sympathetic block), high block, headacheHypotension, accidental dural tap, epidural haematoma (anticoagulants) or abscess → cord compression, local anaesthetic toxicity
  • Contraindications: raised ICP with a mass lesion, coagulopathy, infection at the site, patient refusal.

los.text: Identify the components of the ventricular system and link to the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid and the functional consequences of obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid drainage.
los.html:
1. ProductionChoroid plexus (mainly in the lateral ventricles), ~500 mL/day; ~150 mL present at any time.
2. Lateral ventriclesInterventricular foramina (of Monro) → 3rd ventricle.
3Cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) in the midbrain → 4th ventricle.
4Median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka) → subarachnoid space (cisterns, around the brain and cord).
5Absorption through arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus (venous blood).
ProblemTypeCauses
Block within the ventriclesObstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalusAqueduct stenosis (narrowest point), colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro, posterior fossa tumours, Chiari malformation
Poor absorptionCommunicating hydrocephalusAfter meningitis or SAH (granulations scarred)
Normal pressure hydrocephalusOlder adults: gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, dementia ("wet, wobbly, wacky")
  • Effects: raised ICP (headache worse lying down and in the morning, vomiting, papilloedema, VI palsy)
    • in infants, an enlarging head and bulging fontanelle (sutures open).
    • Treat with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.
  • Never do an LP when obstructive hydrocephalus or a mass is suspected (risk of coning).
